content: Fibrates are a class of amphipathic carboxylic acids used in pharmacology to treat various metabolic disorders, primarily hypercholesterolemia (high cholesterol). They are classified as hypolipidemic agents. For example, fenofibrate (TriCor® in the USA) and fenofibric acid (Trilipix®) are approved by the FDA for use in combination with statins in patients with mixed dyslipidemia. Fibrates are commonly used as adjunctive therapy in different forms of hypercholesterolemia, often in combination with statins. Clinical trials also support their use as monotherapy. While fibrates are less effective at lowering LDL cholesterol, they improve HDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels. Additionally, they appear to enhance insulin resistance in cases of dyslipidemia associated with other features of metabolic syndrome (such as hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus). Various doses of fenofibrate are available on the market, with the standard adult dose typically exceeding 100 mg per day. However, dose adjustments are necessary for patients with renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance < 80 mL/min). Clinical trials are needed to establish the relative efficacy of different fibrate dosages. Fibrates can cause mild gastrointestinal upset and myopathy (muscle pain with elevated creatine phosphokinase levels). When combined with statins, fibrates increase the risk of rhabdomyolysis, a severe condition involving muscle tissue breakdown that can lead to renal failure. Cerivastatin (Lipobay®), a potent statin, was withdrawn from the market due to this complication. Less lipophilic statins are less likely to cause this reaction and are considered safer when used with fibrates. Clofibrate is no longer used because it was associated with increased morbidity and mortality rates, as well as higher malignancy rates in rodent studies. Fibrates are excreted via the kidneys and can cause reversible increases in serum creatinine levels. Therefore, dose reductions are recommended in patients with elevated serum creatinine levels. Gemfibrozil, however, is excreted independently of renal function and can be used in patients with chronic kidney disease. Fibrates have been used clinically since the early 1970s, but their mechanism of action was not fully understood until the 1990s. It was discovered that fibrates activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), particularly PPARα. PPARs are intracellular receptors that regulate carbohydrate and fat metabolism as well as adipose tissue differentiation. Activation of PPARs leads to the transcription of specific genes involved in lipid metabolism, thereby facilitating their therapeutic effects.
